items.title: Barney Bigard Interview, Early 1970s
items.q: when I first joined Duke's band, and he used to arrange so weird, I used to think all these chords were wrong.

ctx.x: Well, now, I know that, uh, today most people have an idea of what the Duke Ellington band sounds like. I mean, the minute you first hear the first few notes, you say, that's Duke Ellington. But I'm sure that when we start playing this next one, that, uh, if we weren't to identify the band, that might take them a bit of a time, unless there are real jazz buffs, to identify this sound. Because this one goes back to, I believe, about 1929, 1930, when Duke Ellington was at the Cotton Club. And we have one called,…

Because it's been so long. But there were good days, you know, and, uh, when I first joined Duke's band, and he used to arrange so weird, I used to think all these chords were wrong. Yeah. And he and I would have the biggest arguments and everything, but he'd prove it was right. And, uh, that's the way he's been. Of all the bands in the country, everybody could always identify Ellington when he came on the air. Right. And during the Depression, everybody wasn't working. Duke was working. Yeah. All through the…
Let's listen to this one. As we said, Duke Ellington, Cotton Club Band, 1930. Shout them, Antilly. Mm-hm. The End The End The End The End The End
When did she come to New York?

Oh, she was there when I was there. I got there -- well, I joined Duke in '27 and I'd been in New York about -- in '25, and I saw her then because I was working with Luis Russell at the place called the Nest.
